笛声长.name: Long Notes of the Flute
笛声长.description:
She was born into the northern frontier's most turbulent years.
In her youth, she was quiet and withdrawn. Her grandfather was perpetually occupied with fort business, leaving her to sit alone in empty rooms, staring blankly so she would not cause trouble for others or gaze enviously at other children who had parents to look after them.
"So long as I shrink my presence and cause no burden, that will be enough."
She always believed this.
Until one day, she heard heated arguments outside: "Old Liu, we'd rather die than hand over iron weapons to the Wuyang!" "Then are you going to let all thousand souls in this fortress perish?" "Coward!" "Fight them to the death!"...
Her grandfather entered, sitting heavily upon the bedside, his broad shoulders hunched as he buried his face in his hands.
The setting sun cast his shadow long and dark across the room, as though the crushing weight of the entire fortress rested upon his back alone.
Her heart tightened; she crept forward and gently stroked the old man's silvering hair, just as he once consoled her. When he looked up, she saw the disheveled trails of tears and grime upon his weary face.
"What can I do?" she asked herself for the first time.
From that day forth, she did her utmost to smile and weave herself into the community. In the mornings, she thanked the uncles keeping watch through the night; in the evenings, she led games for children who had lost their kin. She apprenticed under an old physician, learning to distinguish every medicinal herb and whispering gentle comfort as she bandaged wounds. She also learned to play the flute from an exiled musician, soothing the living and honoring the dead with melody.
Gradually, despair no longer ruled every face in the fortress. Though grain remained scarce and the Wuyang threat loomed, warmth blossomed within this small bastion in a chaotic world.
As dusk fell, the mellow notes of Liu Nian's flute drifted through the evening air. She loved standing on the high ramparts to gaze into the distance.
She knew the sun would rise tomorrow as it always did, and all she had to do was let its light reach every heart.

非吾乡.name: No Home of Mine
非吾乡.description:
Following the conclusion of the Yuankang Northern Expedition, Liu Nian accompanied Sikong Yao south, where she was bestowed the title of Lady Zhaoyi and entered the imperial palace.
Upon first arriving in the southern capital, she saw with her own eyes the misty Jiangnan depicted in ancient scrolls—blue tiles and dark eaves adorning spring hills, while misty weeping willows by the Qinhuai River brushed against the autumn breeze beneath a bright moon.
To say she was not enchanted would be a lie; this fertile land truly nurtured the soul. Yet human nature is ever discontent.
In hardship, she had yearned for tranquility; now that peace was hers, she began to crave what was gone—yearning more and more often for those days in the northern fortress.
Life back then was harsh and meager, yet there was Grandfather, Uncle Qiu, good-natured aunts with ready laughter, and children clamoring for her to play the flute.
Now, everything seemed to have improved, yet she felt further from them than ever. Uncle Qiu seemed changed, as did all those familiar faces; they no longer spoke their hearts to her, and the words in their letters were laden with inescapable reverence, courtesy, and distance.
She tried to hold on to past bonds, yet it felt as futile as grasping at smoke. But she quietly folded these feelings away, keeping them tucked deep within.
The southern capital was nothing like the north: any word or gesture could be weaponized by rival factions. Having little interest in power or opulence, she avoided politics beyond inquiring after old acquaintances in the Beishuo Army, preferring to retreat to her palace chambers for solitude.
Another Mid-Autumn Festival arrived. The southern capital burst into brilliant fireworks, lanterns turning the night into day as townsfolk strolled out to view the moon. Liu Nian ascended the high terrace with the Emperor, sharing wine beneath the moonlight.
When the wine ran dry, flushed cheeks betrayed her intoxication.
Hearing her murmur something while leaning against the balustrade, the Emperor leaned in with curious amusement.
With hazy, wine-dazed eyes, she let out a gentle sigh:
"Bright as day are the streets of the southern capital, yet its twelve jade towers are no home of mine."

历史是一个轮回.name: The Cycle of History
历史是一个轮回.description:
Sikong Xu had never forgotten that half the blame for the death of late Empress Xie Ruolan lay squarely upon his maternal clan, the Chen family. It remained an unbridgeable chasm between himself and the Crown Prince—a poisoned thorn buried deep in his heart for years, impossible to pluck out.
Although Sikong Sheng had made no move against him or his mother over the years—at most having friction over administrative views and governance, and often looking after him like an elder brother—Sikong Xu knew well in his heart that silence and forbearance by no means signified forgiveness.
He understood Sikong Sheng, but that did not mean he would yield.
Just as the Imperial Father could not yield for the sake of the realm back then, Sikong Xu had things he was duty-bound to protect.
No matter how the tides shifted or who triumphed in the end, he would shield his mother and the entire Chen clan whose fate was irrevocably bound to his own.
In a trance, he seemed to see a vast river sweeping everything before it, surging inexorably forward.
Everything, after all, was merely history repeating itself.

近水楼台先得月.name: The Favored Pavilion
近水楼台先得月.description:
Among the myriad court officials, there was no shortage of those who favored the Second Prince, Sikong Xu.
While the Chen clan's influence played a part, it was undeniable that Sikong Xu possessed exceptional talent of his own. From his youth, he displayed extraordinary military genius. During the Longwu Northern Expedition, he took the vanguard himself, slaying enemy generals in the field and achieving illustrious military glory—a degree of valor and strategy unmatched by any other prince.
Compared to Crown Prince Sikong Sheng, who remained secluded in the Eastern Palace and specialized in civil governance, Sikong Xu commanded far greater prestige among the legions. Great Xuan had been founded upon martial might, and the supreme weight of military authority was acknowledged under heaven. Coupled with the fact that his birth mother, Noble Consort Chen, enjoyed deep imperial favor, the Chen clan's disciples and former protégés were entwined throughout the entire bureaucracy.
Crown the eldest, or crown the worthy? Champion civil rule, or champion martial strength? Beneath the court's placid surface, fierce undercurrents surged. Many whispered in secret that this second prince of towering martial deeds might well ascend further.
Yet whenever someone cautiously probed Sikong Xu to pledge allegiance, he always responded with a warm smile and polite deference, showering the Crown Prince with impeccable praise that left no room for fault:
"My imperial brother possesses both virtue and brilliance; he is the undisputed heir of the state. I am but a soldier whose sole wish is to guard the frontiers of Great Xuan. Pray do not harbor improper designs, gentlemen."
Yet when he turned away, his gaze sweeping across the imperial map on his desk and lingering over the towering palace walls, the ambition glinting in the depths of his eyes was sharper than a blade:
"The pavilion nearest the water catches the moonlight first... Imperial Brother, you may hold the title of the eldest, but under heaven, it is the swiftest blade that decides who rules."

暗流.name: Undercurrents
暗流.description:
Elevated to the throne midway as emperor, Sikong Jing understood his predicament better than anyone. The foundation beneath the dragon throne was so precarious that every time he attempted to enact a policy, the entrenched noble clans united to obstruct him.
Grand ambitions to reclaim ancestral lands and establish imperial authority felt too hollow and illusory for him.
He gradually learned silence, burying those unattainable aspirations deep within. Until one early summer, he happened to overhear palace attendants praising the luscious sweetness of lychees from Qingzhou.
"Lychees, is it..."
He murmured softly, seemingly tempted.
In the imperial court, when Sikong Jing proposed digging a grand canal solely to transport lychees, it was unexpectedly met with no fierce opposition. The noble lords exchanged knowing glances—humoring the Emperor was merely the shallowest consideration; what truly mattered was that with the sovereign taking the public blame for such a ruinous and labor-intensive endeavor, the staggering profits of the construction would line all of their pockets.

沉夜.name: Deep Night
沉夜.description:
In the spring of the twenty-fourth year of Yuankang, Emperor Jing of Xuan lay critically ill, his breath faltering day by day, with only months left to live. Under the title of Regent, Eldest Prince Ning, Sikong Zheng, held the affairs of the imperial court firmly in his grasp.
In the dead of night, within the secret chamber of Prince Ning's manor, his trusted confidant Chen Ying lowered his voice:
"Your Highness, this opportunity will slip away in an instant. The Prince of Jin is stationed far on the frontier, beyond reach. If there is merely 'a slight stir' within the inner palace, we may announce the Emperor's sudden demise and forge an imperial edict to assume the throne with full legitimacy."
Candlelight danced across Sikong Zheng's face, revealing the fierce turmoil waging across his brow. He understood Chen Ying's words all too well. That "slight stir" meant snuffing out his father's final thread of life with his own hands—stepping over the blood of his closest kin to seize the pinnacle of power. The crown of dominion was right before his eyes, within an arm's reach.
Before his mind flashed the gaunt face of his father, the broad shoulders that had carried him as a boy, the stern lectures on reviewing memorials... and the calm yet piercing eyes of his younger brother Sikong Yao at the frontlines.
After a long silence, Sikong Zheng slowly closed his eyes. When he opened them once more, the tempest in his gaze had settled. Waving his hand, his voice carried a hint of exhaustion, yet rang crystal clear:
"I refuse. Not merely out of filial duty, nor out of fear of condemnation from all under heaven. If I seize the throne through such vile means, every day and night thereafter will feel like sitting upon needles. I intend to take this realm, but I will take it honorably and uprightly. We shall await Father's passing before advancing our plans."
He chose a path that seemed slower and fraught with peril, staking his wager on time, while preserving a moral line that others might deem laughable.
Chen Ying sighed quietly, speaking no more.
Beyond the window, the night deepened into pitch black.

飘摇.name: Winds of Tumult
飘摇.description:
Sikong Zheng stood atop the high terrace of the newly erected palace gardens, gazing upon the misty silhouettes of pavilions veiled in rain. His right hand instinctively clenched—a hand that had once drawn a three-stone war bow with ease to pierce a willow leaf at a hundred paces.
When the Wuyang breached Yongan, he had shielded his young brother as they fled south, where a stray arrow pierced his shoulder blade amidst the chaos. The arrowhead tore through his tendons; though the wound had long since healed, it still ached with a dull throb whenever the skies turned overcast.
Ever since Father restored the dynasty with the backing of the Chen clan, everything had changed.
He was no longer merely the son of a peripheral prince, but the Eldest Imperial Son of a fledgling court.
This ungrounded regime needed stability, needed grain and silver, and desperately needed the endorsement of the southern aristocrats. The olive branch proffered by the Chen clan—the undisputed leader of the southern nobility—carried an unmistakable message.
He could no longer ride to war for Great Xuan upon the battlefield; thus, he would serve this storm-tossed family through another path.
Securing peace for the realm to give the exiled court breathing room; preserving the precarious legitimacy of the Sikong imperial line; reassuring watchful aristocrats by demonstrating the imperial family's willingness to share power—these were the duties that he, Sikong Zheng, as the eldest son, was compelled to shoulder at this very moment. It was the only choice he could make for his clan and his country.
He forged an alliance with the Chen family—deliberate, composed, and knowing that once that step was taken, there could be no turning back.
Even if it meant shouldering the shameful moniker of "craven appeaser."
The road ahead was long. What could not be resolved in his father's generation might no longer be an insurmountable obstacle once he ascended the throne and Xuan regained its strength...

孤舟行.name: A Solitary Vessel
孤舟行.description:
Throughout court and country, it was common knowledge that Crown Prince Sikong Sheng had been named heir apparent the moment the Emperor ascended the throne; for over a decade, all under heaven seemed to take it for granted that he would succeed the imperial line.
Only Sikong Sheng himself understood that the path beneath his feet had never been smooth.
His mother, the Empress, had passed away early, and power in the inner palace had fallen entirely to Lady Chen, birth mother of the Second Prince. His uncle Xie Xuan secluded himself in his manor, wasting his days in melancholy, while his grandfather Xie Jian'an, despite holding the exalted post of Prime Minister, dared not intervene excessively in state affairs.
An overbearing maternal clan might offer fleeting momentum to a Crown Prince, yet in the long run it remained a lethal hazard—his Imperial Father would never permit Great Xuan to repeat the catastrophic errors of the past.
Thus, from his earliest youth, Sikong Sheng lived as though he were a flawless jade vessel.
He mastered the classics and histories without a single flaw, offering insightful and meticulously reasoned counsel on state affairs; in his conduct toward others, he was gentle, magnanimous, and benevolent. He dared not let his father's eyes betray the slightest disappointment, dared not fall behind his doted-upon second brother in any regard, and dared even less to let the virtuous renown of his late mother be tarnished in the slightest on his account.
Prudence, humility, propriety, and acumen—these became the armor he wore, encasing the fear, loneliness, and exhaustion within so they would never be exposed to the world.
What he carried was far more than the duty of an heir apparent.
It was his late mother's unfulfilled hopes, his father's dream of dynastic resurgence, and the lasting peace of the common folk under heaven.
He walked a solitary, straight road where he could neither veer left nor right, nor ever look back. He had to be perfect, and perfection was his only choice.

烛光明.name: Candlelight in the Dark
烛光明.description:
Another anniversary of his mother's death had arrived. Clad in plain mourning robes, Sikong Sheng stepped into the old Prince of Jin manor at dawn's first light.
"Forgive me for troubling you so early in the morning."
He received the candle offered with both hands by the palace eunuch, his tone so gentle and his manners so impeccable that none could find the slightest fault.
The young eunuch bowed in panic, repeatedly protesting that he was unworthy of such grace.
Speaking no further, Sikong Sheng carefully lit the candle, bowed three times, and knelt quietly upon the prayer mat, watching the flickering flame burn down as he stared at the gilded characters on the spirit tablet: Late Empress Shude Wen.
Only here, within this deserted old residence that held the brief joys of his childhood, could he permit himself to slightly unbind the taut strings of his heart.
In truth, he could no longer recall the exact terror and bewilderment of that childhood chaos; even his mother's face had faded into a soft, hazy silhouette.
Yet he obstinately pursued that feeling—the illusion of being sheltered by his mother, wrapped in utter safety and warmth. Only by chewing upon these faint, phantom remnants of memory could he draw the strength to carry on.
"Your Highness, the hour of the Snake has arrived," the young eunuch's voice drew him back to reality.
Sikong Sheng rose, bowed deeply once more, and turned to depart.
Once he had left the estate, Fan Zhong entered at a measured pace, gazing at the empty doorway with a quiet sigh: "The Crown Prince remains as dutifully filial as ever."
The young eunuch observed Fan Zhong's expression, inquiring tentatively: "Godfather, shall we clear away these freshly lit candles as in previous years?"
"Clear them," Fan Zhong waved his hand. "After all, our rice bowl depends on the masters in the palace."
Moments later, before the spirit tablet of the late Empress Xie, all was pristine and spotless once more.
So spotless... as though no one had ever visited, and as though that guarded, tender longing had never existed at all.

千秋.name: Through the Ages
千秋.description:
When the envoys of the Eastern Yan Murong clan arrived, declaring that the condition for "a joint campaign against the Wuyang to reclaim lost lands" was the hand of the princess in marriage, the first fracture cracked across Sikong Yu's world.
When the news arrived, she was carefully brushing morning dew from an orchid.
Her fingers froze in midair. The chamber suddenly felt terrifyingly still; a bizarre chill seeped into her bones, and all she could hear was the beating of her own heart.
Once, and then once more.
Instinctively, Sikong Yu sought someone to lean on, yet what followed struck like one thunderclap after another.
She heard that her gentle mother, who never contested anything, had removed her hairpins and knelt in the freezing wind outside the Emperor's palace until midnight. She heard that her composed elder brother, the Crown Prince, and her heroic second brother had engaged in a furious dispute over her fate, nearly coming to blows.
That night, dismissing all attendants, Sikong Yu sat alone before the window, countless tangled thoughts weaving through her mind. In the end, only one truth remained crystal clear: her once impregnable sanctuary was on the verge of splintering because of her. Her whimsical worries, set against the colossal collision of dynastic statecraft and family duty, weighed as light as a speck of dust.
As dawn began to break, Sikong Yu drew a deep breath and walked to the desk. Her eyes rested upon the orchid named Thousand Autumns, her lips tightening as she suppressed the lingering regret that she would likely never see it bloom.
On the day the imperial edict was proclaimed, Fan Zhong looked on in astonishment as the Princess personally handed him a painted scroll.
Upon it was an orchid in radiant, breathtaking bloom.
"I have only this to offer Father. May this painting celebrate our Great Xuan—"
"May our rivers and mountains stand unscathed, and our dynasty endure through the ages."
On the day of her departure, the imperial carriage rolled past the gates of the southern capital. As the wind lifted the curtain, she could not resist looking back.
Through blurred tears, she seemed to see a solitary figure standing high upon the battlements, clasping tightly in his hands the very scroll of Thousand Autumns she had painted.
She slowly turned back and sat upright. Ahead lay unfamiliar lands and an uncertain fate.
Yet she was no longer a delicate orchid that only knew how to seek warmth. She was a Princess of Xuan, and with her own brush, she had inscribed herself into the grand tapestry of Great Xuan's enduring ages.

金枝.name: The Golden Branch
金枝.description:
From the day she was born, she had known only benevolence in this world.
Her father's doting love, her mother's tenderness, and the protective care—both clumsy and meticulous—of her two elder brothers had shielded her from every harsh wind. She was like the most precious orchid in the heated conservatory, having never weathered a storm, taking it for granted that whatever she touched would be laid before her eyes.
This potted orchid, named Thousand Autumns, suited her fancy immensely; it was said to be a rare treasure notoriously difficult to nurture. After receiving it, she tended to it daily with her own hands. Watching its emerald leaves glisten translucent beneath the morning light, all she plotted was to present it before her Imperial Father the moment its first flower bloomed, in order to coax the most wondrous reward under heaven from him.
What should she ask for?
Fine silks and satins? Her wardrobes were already overflowing.
Rare jewels and exotic treasures? A simple word would bring them in abundance.
She had even pleaded with her second brother to let her ride spirited steeds in the military camps, and coaxed the Crown Prince to secretly show her the military maps of Xuan's fortresses.
"What should I ask for after all..."
She nudged the budding orchid, grumbling softly with little genuine worry in her heart.
Whether she truly awaited an astonishing, unknown gift, or merely yearned to see the weary brow of her overworked father relax into a warm smile—the Princess kept her own counsel.

孤狼.name: Lone Wolf
孤狼.description:
For as long as Zhu Yuanzhi could remember, he had survived alongside his father—a man reputed to be able to bend horseshoes with his bare hands—scratching out a living in the gray fringes of the frontier. His old man had several sworn brothers who formed a rough band, neither proper soldiers nor common bandits, scraping a living at the tip of the blade: hiring out as caravan escorts one day, and masquerading as horse thieves to plunder solitary travelers the next.
When idle, they ran a blacksmith trade, chiefly reforging illicit weapons into scrap-heaped tools that could be traded without raising eyebrows.
The glowing orange fires of the forge and the metallic stench of blood: that was the entirety of Zhu Yuanzhi's childhood.
Blessed with brute strength, he could swing heavy smithing hammers by age twelve and easily fell grown men in brawls. His father often said this strength was heaven's gift for filling his bowl. In those days, Zhu Yuanzhi, like his father, believed that the strong devouring the weak was simply the way of the world.
Until... the Wuyang tore his rough and savage world to shreds.
His father and all those familiar and unfamiliar faces fell like cut grass. Amidst the slaughter, he hacked his way out through raw ferocity and his intimate knowledge of the terrain, leaving behind a "home" reduced to smoking ash.
From then on he became a lone wolf, wandering south in isolation, struggling through the chaotic world until one rainy night, crazed with hunger, he drew his scimitar to hold up a carriage.
"What a trapped beast."
When four armored guards pinned him to the ground, the carriage curtain parted. The gentleman who would later become his mentor, Chu Huan, did not panic; rather, he chuckled: "Such raw might is wasted on robbing roads."
Zhu Yuanzhi stiffened his neck, attempting to mimic the defiant final words his father had taught him for facing death, but Chu Huan simply waved his guards off: "Take him in. Give him a meal, and find him fresh clothes."

豺狼.name: Pack of Jackals
豺狼.description:
"General, think twice! We cannot deploy! The court's order is merely to repel the Wuyang, not pursue them deep! The Beishuo Army is the dynasty's elite; should we suffer defeat, His Majesty will surely..."
Zhu Yuanzhi did not lose his temper at his strategist; he merely sat slumped in his grand chair, impatiently switching hands as he cleaned his ear. Only when the advisor had rambled himself out did he cut in.
"Finished? You think I'd fight a battle I can't win?"
The strategist was clearly unconvinced, pressing urgently: "General! This is not merely a question of victory! This is..."
"It's about money." Zhu Yuanzhi curled his lip, resting his gaze upon the flickering torchlight, cold clarity veiled deep within his eyes. "With the measly rations the court doles out, the boys are so starved their eyes are practically glowing green. You expect them to tighten their belts and die for you?"
He paused, his voice dropping lower with genuine weight: "Our ranks are packed with refugees who fled down from the north. A fire burns in their guts—they want a better life. If you don't dangle hope in front of them, who's going to bleed for you when it's time to chew through hard bone?"
"Understood? Then go pass the word."
Facing his speech-robbed advisor, he bared his teeth in a grin, a menacing ferocity flashing across his cheerful, rounded face.
"Sound the pursuit! Thirty percent of all plunder goes to the war chest, and the rest is yours to keep! If you have the guts, I'll lead you into Wuyang territory for a feast!"

青山埋骨不埋名.name: Bones in Green Hills, Name in Eternity
青山埋骨不埋名.description:
He had parents, kinsmen, and a wife; in the old Prince of Langya's household, he was merely one among a sea of ordinary retainers.
His escort of Sikong Zheng and Sikong Yao south had less to do with unwavering loyalty and more to do with securing his family's survival and carving out an official career—a matter of self-preservation and calculated opportunism.
Yet after reaching the prosperous and peaceful south, when everything was improving—his official rank climbing steadily and his family enjoying a life far more honorable and lavish than in the north—why did his thoughts begin to shift in silence?
Was it the unintentional condescension of southern aristocrats, treating northerners like second-class rabble, that stung his pride? Was it his southern-born son's utter indifference to northern customs and the memories he held dear that filled him with bitter desolation? Or was it precisely because his homeland was lost forever, never to be seen again, that he longed for it with redoubled fervor?
In the cold prison cell, facing the Chen family's endless enticements and glittering promises, he obstinately bore every accusation alone to shield the Prince of Jin.
Why? For what?
Chu Huan himself did not know.
Nor did his son.
The young man—once obscure and nameless, who after the new Emperor's coronation rose to become the sovereign's most trusted personal bodyguard—stood before Chu Huan's lonely grave.
Only silence answered him.
He had no right to resent or blame; all he could offer was silence.

不画峨眉.name: Forsaking the Painted Brows
不画峨眉.description:
She is the sole female general of Great Xuan, and the only daughter of Great General Zu Kun.
The harsh frontier winds and grinding sands tempered her into iron, and her spear has reaped countless souls among the Wuyang.
"A woman ought to behave like a woman"—such admonitions reached her ears in her early days of martial training, but now, throughout the entire court and country, not a soul dares utter them to her face.
Fourteen when she rode to war beside her father and twenty when she commanded her own army, every single commendation in her military ledger was forged through perilous combat. Backed moreover by the Zu clan—a pillar of Xuan—the worldly rules binding most people were to her nothing more than dust beneath her boots, subordinate only to her father and military law.
Yet despite the noble houses flocking to seek alliance with the illustrious Zu name, Great General Zu Kun still sighs with endless worry whenever trying to arrange a suitable marriage for his daughter.
Whenever the subject is raised, even as Zu Yue stands rigidly at attention before her father, a scornful curl tugs at the corner of her lips:
"Can proper decorum secure the realm? Can refined etiquette reclaim our lost lands? Rather than burdening me with a husband who meddles in my every move, I would sooner have an obedient young lad marry into our house."
And yet, in the quiet depths of the night, this formidable general—whose very name strikes terror into the hearts of her foes—sometimes loses herself gazing at romance novels brought from the south. The painted boats in misty rain and the wind-swept lotuses depicted in those pages brush softly against her heart like spring willow catkins.
She can tame the wildest stallions, yet has never plucked a jade zither; she commands vast tactical formations, yet cannot thread a needle. At times, peering into the mirror and taking in the heroic valor across her brow, she cannot help but wonder: had she been born in an age of peace, might she too have adorned her reflection with floral brocade and strolled beneath an umbrella through the apricot blossoms in spring rain?
"Could one live in peace, who would choose to lick blood from a blade?" at a victory banquet, she had once sighed deeply. "I too would like little bridges over flowing streams; I would like to learn the zither and compose verse, and best of all, to have a handsome gentleman at my side."
Led by Xie Xuan, several generals in the tent burst into roaring laughter, dismissing it as nothing more than drunken jesting.

安能折腰.name: How Could She Bend
安能折腰.description:
Zu Yue led her vanguard to relieve Yiyang, yet with General Chen Ying holding the Xiangzhou garrison back, the city stood on the precipice of doom.

To save thousands of besieged soldiers and a city of innocent civilians, Zu Yue—whose spine had always been forged of unyielding pride—rode alone into Chen Ying's military camp.

Confronted with Chen Ying's petty obstruction and blatant extortion for battlefield glory, Zu Yue knew well his narrow, selfish nature: without guaranteed spoils and credit, he would never risk his troops.

"General Chen! If you march to complete the encirclement at once, the primary merit of victory will be yours, the glory of slaying the enemy commander will be yours, and every scrap of captured plunder shall belong entirely to your division!"

Chen Ying eyed the famously proud tiger-daughter of the Zu clan sideways. Seeing her clench her teeth, her fists trembling slightly as she contained her fury, a smug malice welled within his heart.
"General Zu, words alone carry no weight."

Fury flared in Zu Yue's eyes like blazing embers. Yet before her mind's eye flashed the vision of her comrades bleeding upon the parapets of Yiyang and the desperate tears of the townsfolk. Closing her eyes, she took a long, deep breath, lifted her battle robes, and sank heavily onto one knee:
"The military plight of Great Xuan is dire beyond measure. In the name of ten thousand living souls in Yiyang, Zu Yue implores General Chen to deploy!"

That single kneel was for the common folk of Great Xuan; it shattered the lifelong pride she had held.

Shaken by her fierce resolve, Chen Ying finally issued the order to march. The siege of Yiyang was broken, and news of grand triumph was dispatched to the court. While Chen Ying basked in boastful arrogance, Zu Yue quietly tended to her wounded troops without contesting a single word of credit.

Years later, when someone dared ask her of that day, Zu Yue took a hearty swig of fiery wine and laughed boldly:
"Every bone in my body kneels only to Heaven, Earth, and my Sovereign Father. But if bending my knee can save a whole city and preserve thousands of my brothers-in-arms from slaughter, what is a momentary bow? Even had it cost Zu Yue's head, I would not have hesitated for a heartbeat!"

君臣陌路.name: Sovereign and Subject Estranged
君臣陌路.description:
On the Lantern Festival of the third year of Longwu, carriages lined the street outside the Xie manor in an unbroken procession. As the imperial father-in-law, maternal grandfather to the Crown Prince, Grand Situ, Prime Minister, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, and Governor of Jingzhou, Xie Jian'an had reached the pinnacle of ministerial power. Yet the higher his authority climbed, the deeper the dread gnawed at his heart.
Ever since the new Emperor ascended the throne, the Xie clan had flourished under imperial patronage, even rivaling the Chen clan for supremacy among southern aristocrats. Yet measured against the deep foundations of the Chen house, the Xie clan still fell short. However, it was no easy task for the Chen family to suppress the Xie either. After several covert clashes, both sides gradually conceived different thoughts, walking tacitly toward another direction.
Today, when the Chen envoy arrived to offer festival greetings, he tentatively proposed a marriage alliance between the younger generations of both houses. Xie Jian'an did not agree on the spot, nor did he refuse, merely remarking that he would consider the matter.
He understood the implicit signal all too well. Though his daughter's death remained an unhealable wound in his heart, he was not merely a grieving father; he was the patriarch of a clan, duty-bound to weigh the survival of his kin. Continuing a bloody feud with the Chen clan would indeed earn him imperial favor for now, but in the long run, how could the Emperor ever tolerate another "Chen clan"?
Xie Jian'an had counseled this sovereign for far too long; he understood the ruler's mind better than anyone else. A monarch of such grand ambition and ruthless vision would never permit aristocratic clans to grow unchecked.
What was worse, the Xie were an imperial consort clan—an added death warrant hanging above their heads.
Xie Jian'an poised his brush, hesitated, and let blobs of ink spoil several sheets of fine stationery.
After a long silence, he finally finished a reply and dispatched a servant to the Chen manor.
Watching the servant hurry off with the letter, the study fell quiet. Closing the window shutters, all that lingered was a solitary sigh:
"The affairs of this world are like a game of chess..."

当断则断.name: Decisive Severance
当断则断.description:
Inside an ordinary residence in the capital.
Clad in a black robe, Xie Jian'an knocked upon the gate.
A long-waiting confidant swiftly summarized the latest rumors and political shifts in the capital for him.
Matters had escalated to such a pitch that there was no room left for hesitation or looking back.
After brief deliberation, Xie Jian'an dismissed his confidant. Searching out paper and brush from the room, he tested his stroke several times before finally setting ink to parchment—imitating Chen Dao's calligraphy to write four bold, vigorous characters:
"Execute the Prince of Jin."
Gazing upon those four words, his sagging, wrinkled eyelids drooped, cloaking the chill in his gaze.
Whether the Chen clan truly harbored such intentions was irrelevant; nor did the actual desires of Prince Ning and Chen Dao matter.
He needed only to pave a stepping stone for his imperial son-in-law, and then... deliver a gentle push amidst these treacherous undercurrents.
Blowing the ink dry, he tucked the slip carefully into his breast pocket, pushed open the door, and vanished briskly into the night.

君子不立危墙下.name: A Noble Shuns the Falling Wall
君子不立危墙下.description:
As a sweeping campaign of political reform unfolded, Xie Xuan, as its principal architect, saw his status soar.
Yet as the saying goes, high places are fraught with bitter cold; danger gathered steadily in the shadows of the dynasty.
"Marquis, your father has sent yet another letter, urging you to halt and return to the capital."
His subordinate waited anxiously for over an hour with a distressed face, yet Xie Xuan never so much as looked up, entirely immersed in reviewing memorials on the new laws. This was the seventh family letter in six months, and once again, he chose to ignore it.
The sages taught that a noble man does not stand beneath a crumbling wall. Xie Xuan was no fool; he knew well the perils that lay ahead.
Severing a man's fortune is like slaying his parents; having crossed so many entrenched interests, the memorials demanding his impeachment could easily bury the Emperor's desk. Yet if he stepped back now, what would become of the humble scholars seeking a path upward? What would become of the displaced northern folk struggling to survive? And what would his sister's sacrifice have been for?
Xie Xuan understood that his imperial brother-in-law on the dragon throne was using his ties of blood to his sister and the Crown Prince to drive him forward, turning him into a sharp blade pointed straight at the aristocracy.
Yet paving the way for Sheng'er was not wrong, and giving voice to the common folk was all the more righteous.
Xie Xuan finally set down his brush and paced to the window. The night was thick, the solitary moon hung cold.
Suddenly he let out a low chuckle—self-deprecating, yet ringing with unyielding resolve.
"Reply to my father," his voice was calm: "Tell him... it is not that I do not know how to retreat, but that I cannot."
When a true man acts, he does not ask if he can, but whether he should.
For Xie Xuan today, his entire creed was summed in four words:
No backing down!

鲜衣怒马少年郎.name: Youth in Silken Robes and Spirited Steeds
鲜衣怒马少年郎.description:
In the aristocratic circles of the capital, Xie Xuan had always been a figure of great notoriety.
Unlike ordinary scions of prominent houses, Xie Xuan cared little for philosophical debates or metaphysical contemplation, yet he was never absent from righteous brawls or lively commotions. His father, Xie Jian'an, was utterly helpless; in the end, he threw up his hands and pulled strings to pack him off to Great General Zu Kun's army.
For one, he hoped the grueling discipline of military life would beat some sense into the boy, sending him back to the capital to study poetry and carry on the Xie family's scholarly lineage.
And second, his son was blessed with fine looks and a passing grasp of tactics; General Zu happened to have a daughter of comparable age, did he not?
Yet for all his calculating, sending him there was like throwing meat to a dog—he never looked back.
In the army, Xie Xuan took to the life like a fish to water. Armed with boundless family wealth, silver paved his way as he rode the finest steeds, drank the fiercest wine, wore the sharpest blade, hunted down the most ruthless Wuyang bandits, and hit it off splendidly with General Zu's daughter. Whenever he was bested in the drill grounds, he would shout defiance with one breath—"Wait till my brother-in-law gets here, he'll beat you black and blue!"—while graciously conceding defeat with the next, walking the perimeter showering silver on spectating soldiers while bellowing, "Zu Yue is my auntie!"
Though wild and unruly, brazenly fearless under the shelter of his minister father and consort sister, his valor in battle was terrifyingly fierce. In the early days, Minister Xie nearly fainted whenever he received reports of Xie Xuan charging enemy lines and suffering grave wounds; over time, he grew numb, only able to grit his teeth whenever a letter arrived:
"Tally the medicinal herbs in our storehouses, and send them to General Zu."

岂在朝朝与暮暮.name: Beyond the Passing Days
岂在朝朝与暮暮.description:
Even among highborn daughters of noble houses, Xie Ruolan was regarded as a paragon of grace and virtue. Raised in the illustrious Xie clan amidst wealth and honor, she was tutored in the zither, chess, calligraphy, and painting, steeped in poetry and cultural refinement. When her father, Xie Jian'an, informed her of the clan's decision to betroth her to the Prince of Jin, Sikong Yao, though she had long known her fate was not hers to command, a quiet desolation gripped her heart.
He was an imperial prince whose name she had barely heard; from the idle gossip of her salon companions, she could only piece together a cold, austere silhouette.
She had envisioned her future husband as an elegant scholar of refined discourse, or a dashing general of the frontier; she had never imagined an unremarkable prince who was neither the eldest son nor marked by any distinguished achievement.
"Ruolan, trust your father in this matter. The Prince of Jin is no ordinary dragon bound to a pond. Furthermore... it is easy to add flowers to brocade, but rare to deliver charcoal in the snow. If our Xie clan wishes to rise higher, taking the beaten path will not suffice."
Looking into the uncompromising depths of her father's eyes, all her sorrow and confusion dissolved into an almost imperceptible sigh.
...
Inside the Prince of Jin's manor, Xie Ruolan looked at the wooden casket in her hands, packed with a stack of letters that for various reasons had never been dispatched.
She lowered her gaze to the elegant script she had penned:
"I pray this finds you well. The northern frontier is bitter cold; pray add more clothes."
"All is peaceful within the manor. A thousand leagues apart, we share the same bright moon."
"Turmoil brews in the capital. My lord should return with haste."
This political marriage between two strangers—when had it begun to change?
Perhaps it shifted with every bit she learned of the Prince of Jin, with the quiet accommodations woven into daily life, and with each solemn promise he fulfilled without fail...
Xie Ruolan read through the letters one by one, until she reached the final page.
Drawing a breath, she held the paper above the flame of the candle.
She watched the tongues of fire lick across the parchment, reducing every trace of her longing, concern, and anxiety to ash.
Including the two hurried characters scrawled across that final letter:
"Do not return."

明月千里与君同.name: One Moon Across a Thousand Leagues
明月千里与君同.description:
In the spring of the twenty-fourth year of Yuankang, news of the fall of Dongming City exploded like thunder across the entire capital.
Everyone understood that Prince Ning's faction was finished; save for a desperate few who could not jump ship, the vast majority began weighing their options for tomorrow.
Before the armies arrived, hearts had already scattered.
"My Lady, the Prince has... taken Dongming City."
Inside the Prince of Jin's manor, the maid A'Jiao's voice carried an unmistakable tremor.
Xie Ruolan sat poised at her desk, steadily sealing the final letter with wax.
"Deliver these letters to the various yamens and residences on this list. Tell them that if they continue to straddle the fence and hesitate, their names will be the first presented to the Prince when he returns to the capital."
Her tone was gentle, yet A'Jiao bit her lip as she took the thick stack of correspondence, unable to hold back a worried plea: "Could this invite even greater peril? Your Ladyship is already walking on a blade's edge; why take the risk yourself to provoke Prince Ning..."
Hearing the genuine concern in her words, Xie Ruolan's eyes curved softly.
"Prince Ning's heavy guard will seal off this manor shortly; we have little time left."
Soothing her maid's nerves, she looked out the window at the bright moon hanging high in the sky.
Was her hero, a thousand leagues away, looking upon that same moon and thinking of her?
"My personal safety is a trifle. If Xuan continues to bleed from this internal strife, so that the frontier is destabilized and foreign foes strike... that would be a sin I could never atone for in ten thousand deaths."
Not merely for this crumbling dynasty, she was the one who stood shoulder-to-shoulder with him, not one to cower in his shadow.
She would sweep the path clear for him, even if it took intimidation, bribery, and walking into the jaws of peril.

且待风雨来.name: Awaiting the Approaching Storm
且待风雨来.description:
Incense smoke curled within the Phoenix Wutong Palace as a trusted court maid swiftly reported the latest moves from the outer court in hushed tones.
The elder statesmen of the aristocracy, led by the Xue and Tang clans, were joining hands with their disciples to press Crown Prince Sikong Sheng step by step in the Hall of the Supreme Ultimate.
"My Lady," the maid's voice thrummed with irrepressible excitement, "this is a gift from heaven! The clan elders suggest that Your Ladyship watch from the sidelines. Once the Crown Prince stumbles and is blamed for sabotaging the Northern Expedition, his prestige will collapse! He may lose imperial favor altogether, and with our Second Prince's towering martial deeds and Your Ladyship's backing, what great ambition could fail!"
She did not answer. The hall fell into silence. The maid kept her eyes obediently cast to the floor, yet behind her hovered countless unseen eyes, focusing their eager expectations upon her.
In truth, she had little need to choose—she already stood upon the winning side of the scale. Yet when she finally broke the silence, her voice was calm and brook no contradiction:
"Prepare my robes."
Adorning herself in golden hairpins and grand ceremonial attire, she ascended the stairs toward the Hall of the Supreme Ultimate. Sunlight bathed her figure in gold, only to be swallowed by the shadows of the palace doors. Two files of silent, grim soldiers followed in her wake, their armor glinting with cold iron.
Clan interests were certainly vital, and she yearned for her son's triumph. But while Sikong Yao bled on the frontlines, she would never sit idly by as his life's work was reduced to ashes, nor could she permit Great Xuan to miss its golden chance at imperial hegemony over internal factional strife.
That was not the conduct of a statesman of the realm, and still less what Chen Wan'er desired in her heart!
Her skirts sweeping the floor, she stepped into the Hall of the Supreme Ultimate with regal grace. Every step was resolute, every step decisive.
When he returned victorious, would he be grateful for her securing his rear, or fearful of her meddling in state power? She harbored no naive optimism.
Yet she had no regrets.
The Northern Expedition had to succeed. And into the bedrock of that victory would be carved the bloody blade she struck today.
As for what the future held—
Let the storm come.

泥沼染浊色.name: Tainted by the Mire
泥沼染浊色.description:
In the seventh year of Longwu, elder statesman Chen Lang passed away after serving three reigns. The Emperor bestowed upon him supreme posthumous honors and noble titles. Simultaneously, rumors regarding the elevation of an empress grew louder in the capital.
All under heaven knew that in this dynasty, only the Emperor's first wife—late Empress Shude Wen of the Xie clan, who had passed away before his coronation—had ever held the phoenix throne.
And today, the figure of highest distinction in the inner palace was none other than Lady Chen.
Letting idle gossip wash over her ears like a passing jest, Chen Wan'er waved her confidant away and raised her brush to compile the new Precepts for Women.
To speak candidly, having arrived at this day, to claim she harbored no desire for the empress's seat would be self-deception. Yet she knew in her heart that she might never touch that position in this lifetime. After all, how can the living compete with the dead?
Even now, she could not help but remember that gentle, serene woman, remembering her words: "Take Sheng'er and go." She recalled rushing to the Prince of Jin's manor to secure for the Chen clan the paramount merit of "rescuing the imperial heir"—rather than saving both mother and son and altering the future balance of the inner palace and aristocracy. She had even rehearsed the argument in her mind:
How she would lay bare the stakes, how she would depict the crisis...
Yet when those clear eyes gazed upon her, offering the exact outcome she desired before she could utter a word, the tight strings in her chest snapped slack—followed by a wave of guilty, dark, remorse-laden relief.
When her father died abruptly, she was the chip her granduncle used to appease the clan elders; when the Chen clan backed the wrong faction, she became the pact of mutual exploitation between aristocracy and imperial house. She knew good from evil, understood right from wrong, and possessed a clear sense of self, yet she willingly bound herself in chains to the name "Chen," never once escaping the cage to attain true freedom.
It was so then; it was so now.
Her brush paused. The gathered ink finally dripped down, sullying the delicate calligraphy she had just written. Staring at the ink stain, Chen Wan'er seemed to see the complex hue of her entire life—a color stained with calculation and guilt, forever impossible to wash clean.

慕容崔.name: Murong Cui
慕容崔.description: Murong Cui is an exalted prince of the Murong clan holding dominion over Eastern Yan. Despite his noble imperial birth, he never idled in court luxury; rather, through extraordinary military genius and illustrious battlefield triumphs against the Wuyang, he became Eastern Yan's youngest and most celebrated general, commanding immense renown throughout the court and realm.
